We would like to complement our initial rebuttal regarding the novelty of our work, following the separate discussions with the reviewers outlined below.

After a careful review of the recently published and preprint papers on search-and-score methods for ancestral graphs, it appears that none of the existing methods have been benchmarked on anything other than continuous datasets derived from linear Gaussian models.

Therefore, our search-and-score method, which is designed to analyze challenging categorical datasets, is quite unique in this regard and has been properly benchmarked against the state-of-the-art implementation (ref 41) of the reference causal discovery method, FCI (see revised Fig 2 and novel Fig 3). In fact, our method is clearly complementary to all existing methods (with both published and unpublished codes), as it is the only search-and-score method with a demonstrated capacity to discover ancestral graphs from categorical datasets.

We thank you again for your interest in this work.

We are sorry if some of our responses were a "bit hard to follow". We have made our best to reply to each reviewer's questions, while linking some of our responses to avoid excessive redundancy. 

In our rebuttal, we addressed in full transparency your only question to "more clearly delineate what is novel and different here as compared to the other recent works of search-and-score for ancestral graphs".

You now suggest, one day before the end of the discussion period, that we should have performed additional experiments by 1) somehow forcing the comparison with existing search-and-score methods designed for continuous gaussian datasets (instead of categorical data) and 2) requesting unpublished codes to colleagues in direct conflict of interest!

While we have clearly acknowledged the existence and merit of existing methods in our paper, it is not so "simple" and clearly no longer possible to perform such comparisons, after the rebuttal period. Indeed, our method relies on scores combining both conditional multivariate informations and symmetrized fNML complexity costs (see eg Table 1). While there are well known relations between partial correlations and conditional multivariate information for Gaussian datasets, as alluded to by this reviewer, it is not so "simple" to adapt fNML complexity costs for categorical variables to continuous Gaussian variables. 

As outlined in our rebuttal, extension to continuous data will be done in due course, while circumventing at the same time the restriction to Gaussian datasets, but it is clearly beyond this first manuscript focusing on categorical variables. Besides, comparing methods designed to analyze such different types of data (ie continuous Gaussian versus categorical variables) could hardly be seen as fair in the present manuscript.

__Q1.__ _Are the limitations related to the cap of two-collider paths only? Are there any issues related to computational complexity? This was partially referenced in the attached form._

→ We thank this reviewer for emphasizing the main strengths of our work. The cap of two-collider paths does not result from some computational complexity issue, but rather from a deliberate choice of implementing the simplest approximation for the likelihood score of ancestral graphs. In principle, this cap could be extended to longer collider paths without major conceptual nor practical difficulties (using for instance depth-first search algorithm to find all multi-collider paths in linear time), but this was not our objective here (see also our reply to reviewer Rzut concerning approximate versus “exact score”).  

→ Beyond the two-collider cap, another limitation, we will mention in the final manuscript, concerns the current restriction to categorical data only. While it is beyond the present manuscript, we intend to adapt MIIC_search&score to analyze continuous and mixed-type data as well, based on MIIC existing framework to analyze such data (Cabeli et al Why21@NeurIPS 2021, Cabeli et al PloS Comput Biol 2020, Ribeiro-Dantas et al iScience 2024). 
     
__Q2.__ _What was the reason of choosing only three models for benchmarks? It is unclear the actual advantage of such approach w.r.t. the existing FCI algorithm._

→ As mentioned in the general reply to all reviewers’ comments, we have improved the implementation of the method (fixing also a bug) and extended its experimental benchmarking, which resulted in improved performance on precision and recall, especially at small sample sizes, as shown in the revised Fig 2 (see uploaded pdf).
 
→ We have also added a new challenging benchmark from the bnlearn repository (Mildew 35 nodes, 46 edges, 540,150 parameters), which shows similar performance trends as with the 3 initial benchmarks, see revised Fig 2. 

→ In addition, we have now performed a bootstrap sensitivity analysis of sampling noise for all 4 benchmarked models, based on independent resamplings with replacement of single datasets of increasing size, see new Fig 3 in the uploaded pdf. However, FCI could only converge on these bootstrapped datasets for Alarm (on all sample sizes tested) and Insurance (for N$\leqslant$1,000) explaining the lack of FCI comparison with MIIC and MIIC_search&score in all other cases. 

→ Interestingly, the “error bars” in Fig 2 reflect the variance of each method across independently drawn datasets, while the typically smaller “error bars” in Fig 3 reflect the variance of each method across independent resamplings with replacement of a specific dataset for each sample size. Hence, Fig 3 highlights not only the robustness against resampling noise but also the difference in performance across methods for a specific (resampled) dataset. By contrast, the typically larger variances observed in Fig 2 tend to mask the actual performance difference across methods by highlighting the overlaps between the worse results of the best method (_ie_ for the less informative datasets) and the best results of the worse method (_ie_ for the most informative datasets).

→ All in all, Fig 2 and Fig 3 demonstrate that MIIC_search&score significantly outperforms FCI on both precision and recall on small datasets (_eg_ <10,000 samples), while showing similar performance at larger sample size, as expected from the asymptotic consistency of FCI for very large datasets. Hence, these results highlight MIIC_search&score capacity to learn complex graphical models from limited available data, which is a frequent setting for many reald-world datasets, in practice. 

__Q3.__ _Why keeping the sample size range fixed even if the number of possible states increases dramatically? Observing 100 samples for BARLEY means that (ideally) each algorithm observe less than 1% of the state space, which limits the experimental evidence._

→ We have now performed benchmarks on larger datasets including 50,000 samples, which show very similar results between FCI and MIIC_search&score. We outline them below in terms of MIIC_search&score (and FCI)  Fscores for 0% to 20% of latent variables:
- Alarm 0%: 0.93 (0.96), 5%: 0.93 (0.94), 10%: 0.92 (0.95), 20%: 0.89 (0.85)
- Insurance 0%: 0.94 (0.90), 5%: 0.88 (0.85), 10%: 0.83 (0.84), 20%: 0.84 (0.82) 
- Barley 0%: 0.77 (0.77), 5%: 0.76 (0.74), 10%: 0.74 (0.73), 20%: 0.60 (0.61) 
- Mildew 0%: 0.78 (0.79), 5%: 0.74 (0.81), 10%: 0.72 (0.78), 20%: 0.61 (0.75) 

Hence FCI and MIIC_search&score tend to have similar performance on these large datasets, as expected from FCI’s asymptotic consistency on very large datasets, as discussed above. 

→ As pointed out by this reviewer, it is true that benchmaking causal discovery methods using even 50,000 samples is not enough to explore the whole set of parameters of complex models, such as Barley (48 nodes, 84 edges, 114,005 parameters) or Mildew (35 nodes, 46 edges, 540,150 parameters). However, learning model parameters is not actually the goal of causal discovery methods, which “only” aim at learning graph structures (_ie_ their list of edges) given a usually limited number of samples, as in biological or biomedical applications. As Fig 2 and Fig 3 show, learning simple graph structures of complex models (in terms of parameter space) is more difficult than learning graph structures of less complex models. This is however clearly not impossible, given the good precision and recall scores reached even for Barley and Mildew models, despite the comparatively more limited amount of data relative to the state space of these two models. This is especially encouraging, in our view, for the perspective of learning simplified models from complex yet inevitably limited data in real-world applications.

__Q1.__ _Can the authors more clearly delineate what is novel and different here as compared to the other recent works of search-and-score for ancestral graphs?_

→ Concerning the overlaps of our work with recent papers and preprints on search-and-score methods for ancestral graphs, we actually discovered these papers and preprints during the final wrap up of the present manuscript. In fact, as pointed out in our reply to reviewer NFNu, there are clear differences of formulation between our work based on ac-connection criterion and published or submitted works relying on m-separation/connection criterion and head-and-tail factorization. 

→ In full transparency, our main theoretical result, namely the likelihood decomposition of ancestral graphs in terms of “ac-connected subsets” (Theorem 1), was already included in a very similar form in a 2017 submission by one of us to the UAI conference.  The main difference was that Theorem 1 was incorrectly stated in terms of multivariate information instead of multivariate _cross_-information. This incorrect Theorem 1 (now corresponding to Proposition 3 in the present lately revised manuscript) was numerically shown to be erroneous by an astute UAI reviewer in 2017. This explains our present emphasis on carefully distinguishing multivariate cross-information from multivariate information (see Appendix C for a detailed discussion). 

→ From an application perspective, MIIC_search&score is also different from most existing search-and-score methods for ancestral graphs which only apply to continuous data assuming multivariate Gaussian distributions. It is the case of refs 11-13 as well as Tsirlis _et al_ 2018 and Bhattacharya _et al_ 2021, whose codes could not be included in our benchmarks focusing on complex datasets over categorical variables.  In addition, the few search-and-score methods for ancestral graphs, that are not limited to continuous multivariate Gaussian data, such as refs 30 and 32, do not provide a code, which could be included in our benchmark comparisons. 

→ While this is beyond the present manuscript, MIIC_search&score will eventually be extended to analyze continuous data (without assuming Gaussian distributions) as well as mixed-type data, combining continuous and categorical variables, based on the existing capability of MIIC algorithm to tackle such data (see Cabeli _et al_ PloS Comput Biol 2020, Cabeli _et al_ Why21@NeurIPS 2021, Ribeiro-Dantas _et al_ iScience 2024).

__Q1.__ _What is the main Novelty of Theorem 1 compared to [14]? Can the theoretical motivation for the proposed search-and-score algorithm be deduced from the results in [14]?_

→ Hu and Evans 2020 (ref 14) proposed polynomial algorithms to find the Markov equivalence class of MAGs and ADMGs. This reference is therefore of clear interest to motivate new search and score algorithms to learn such graphs. Concerning Theorem 1, we only recently discovered its connection to Hu and Evans 2020 (ref 14). Their Proposition 3.3 is, in fact, formulated quite differently from our Theorem 1. On the one hand, Proposition 3.3 is based on m-separation criterion with a proof relying on head-and-tail factorization. On the other hand, Theorem 1 does not rely on head-and-tail factorization anywhere and introduces the concept of ac-connected subsets of variables, which readily translates into an effective decomposition and estimation of the cross-entropy of ancestral graphs. We further address the genesis of Theorem 1 in our reply to reviewer mHLp, below.

__Q2.__ _Do you have convergence guarantees for the algorithm? In other words, how many edge orientations need to be probed before convergence in step 1? How many loops over nodes and edges are needed until convergence?_

→ Yes, both step 1 and step 2 of the algorithm have convergence guarantees, based on a deterministic greedy search and the monitoring of the decrease of global node and edge scores until convergence or a finite limit cycle. In practice, the number of loops over nodes and edges until convergence is rather limited, reaching typically 1 to 2 loops for nodes (step 1) and 3 to 6 loops for edges (step 2) on the 4 benchmarked models tested here (_ie_ Alarm, Insurance, Barley and the new benchmark Mildew, see revised Fig 2 uploaded as pdf).

__Q3.__ _Is there any class of distributions or graphs for which algorithm is guaranteed to converge to a true hidden causal graph?_

→ This is an interesting but difficult question! One could expect that the algorithm restricted to two-collider paths would be guaranteed to converge to the true hidden causal graph, provided the latter only contains up to two-collider paths. However, as discussed in the paper, the “exact score” in terms of multivariate information is actually an “estimate" of the true cross-entropy and its exact decomposition into multivariate cross-information over ac-connected subsets (Theorem 1 and Appendix C). Hence, there might not be any guarantee of convergence to the true ancestral graph, in the infinite sample size limit, even with an algorithm including collider-paths of any length. Yet, for actual applications on real-world finite datasets, we believe that approximate search-and-score methods such as MIIC_search&score are still useful to learn more reliable graphical models including hidden causal variables.

__Q4.__ _Did you perform any experiment to understand how sensitive is the proposed algorithm to the noise?_

→ We thank this reviewer for this suggestion. We have now performed a bootstrap sensitivity analysis to sampling noise for all 4 benchmarked models, based on independent resamplings with replacement of single datasets of increasing size, see new Fig 3 in the uploaded pdf. As can be seen from these plots, MIIC_search&score (as well as original MIIC) appear fairly robust to resampling noise, while FCI could only converge for Alarm (on all sample sizes tested) and Insurance (for N$\leqslant$1,000). This explains the lack of FCI comparison with MIIC and MIIC_search&score in all other cases for these bootstrapped datasets. We further discuss these results in our reply to reviewer 2yrv.

→ We would also like to address this reviewer’s concern about the presumed higher sensitivity to noise when considering higher order multivariate cross-information terms. It is true that multivariate cross-information over large sets of variables are more sensitive to noise, as the dataset must be split into smaller and smaller subsets to estimate multivariate joint distributions across more and more variables. Yet, these high order contributions only account for a (small) part of the global cross-entropy, in general, as many contributions come in fact from small ac-connected subsets of variables. Besides, note that the original MIIC algorithm, although limited to v-structure (triple) motifs, already computes conditional multivariate information over possibly large number of variables, such as $I(X;Y;A_n|\set{A_i}_{n-1})$ in Eq.13. See also further discussion about the complexity cost associated to multivariate information contributions from large ac-connected subsets in our reply to Reviewer Rzut. 

__Q5.__ _In the first step of the algorithm does it matter in which order vertices are processed? do you select any specific order?_

→ No the algorithm is both node order and edge order independent, as all the updates are done at the end of each iteration once all the node scores (step 1) or edge scores (step 2) have been estimated.

__Q1.__ _Could authors elaborate more on where Theorem 1 can be applied?_

→ We would like to thank this reviewer for underlining the importance of the topic and the clarity of our paper. Concerning this first question, we are not sure to understand the meaning of “where Theorem 1 can be applied”? Theorem 1 can be applied to learn graphical models including possible unobserved latent variables, that are ubiquitous in many real-world applications.  In practice, one simple way to apply Theorem 1 and compute the contributions of ac-connected subsets is to split them into strictly bayesian contributions (_ie_ ignoring bidirected edges), by summing over all the nodes conditioned on their parents, and into complementary contributions partitioned into collider paths including an increasing number of bidirected edges.

__Q2.__ _I am curious about how to find ac-connected subset, and what the computational complexity is._

→ This is an interesting question, which we have not explored in detail in this paper as we have deliberately restricted our implementation to small and simple ac-connected subsets, including up to two-collider paths only, which do not pose any particular computational complexity issues. 

→ While this approach could be extended to include longer collider paths, the computational complexity for finding all ac-connected subsets, including those with disconnected subsets (see Fig 1G), will be higher although not exponential. Indeed, the Markov equivalence class of ancestral graphs can actually be found in polynomial time (_eg_ Ref 14). Moreover, in practice, the complexity can always be bounded by restricting the maximum connectivity degree and the maximum length of collider paths. 

__Q3.__ _One important thing that the readers may wonder is, what is the performance difference between the method based on approximate local scores limited to the closed surrounding vertices and the method with exact scores. Could the authors present more clues?_

→ The current approximation is the same as the “exact score”, as long as there are no collider paths including two or more bidirected edges. Otherwise, it is possible to enumerate the ac-connected contributions between the approximate and exact scores. For instance, for the toy Model 3 of Fig 3 (initial submitted version), the difference between the approximate and exact scores amounts to the following additional multivariate information contributions in the exact score, 
$$I(X_1;X_2;X_4;X_6;X_7) - I(X_1;X_2;X_4;X_6;X_7;X_5)  =  I(X_1;X_2;X_4;X_6;X_7|X_5)$$ 

corresponding to the 3-collider path $X_1 \rightarrow X_2\leftrightarrow X_4 \leftrightarrow X_6\leftarrow X_7$ without or with the additional directed edge $X_5 \rightarrow X_4$.
While these multivariate information contributions can readily be estimated for categorical data, an fNML complexity “correction” should also be added to take into account the model complexity, as for the symmetrized fNML complexity of the edge scores, corresponding to conditional mutual information contributions, in Table 1. While we have not computed such symmetrized fNML complexity terms beyond two-collider paths, a simple (over)estimate can be readily obtained using BIC complexity, 
$$I(X_1;X_2;X_4;X_6;X_7|X_5) + {1\over 2}(r_1-1)(r_2-1)(r_4-1)(r_6-1)(r_7-1)r_5{\log N\over N}$$
This product of levels along the collider path suggests that the (negative) multivariate conditional information contributions  from long collider paths should be eventually outweighed by their (positive) complexity cost for finite datasets, thereby providing a natural bound, so that high scoring ancestral graph models tend to contain rather short collider paths in practice.

__Q4.__ _Could the authors present some efficiency comparisons empirically, as the authors say "to implement an efficient and reliable heuristic method applicable to more challenging graphical modes and large datasets"._

→ Unfortunately, no comparison could be made with other search-and-score methods on the presented ancestral graph benchmarks for categorical datasets (_i.e._ Alarm, Insurance, Barley and the newly added Mildew benchmarks). Indeed, as already pointed out in our reply to reviewer mHLp, available search-and-score methods  can only analyze continuous (preferentially Gaussian) datasets (_eg_ refs 11-13) or do not provide a code (_eg_ refs 12, 30, 32). Note that MIIC_search&score will eventually be extended to also tackle continuous and mixed-type data, as discussed in our reply to reviewer mHLp, but this was beyond the present manuscript.

summary.value:
The paper proposes a greedy search-and-score algorithm for causal structure discovery in ancestral graphs which allow for both directed and bidirected edges.The paper provides an explicit decomposition of the likelihood function of ancestral graphs
in terms of multivariate cross-information over relevant ‘ac-connected’ subsets of variables which is related to head-and-tail factorization developed in prior work. In the main theoretical result authors show that cross-entropy and the likelihood function of an ancestral graph can be decomposed in terms of multivariate cross-information for ac-connected components. As a corollary this implies that two ancestral graphs are Markov equivalent if and only if they have the same ac-connected subsets of vertices.
Authors use the likelihood function decomposition in terms of cross-information of ac-connected componenetsto propose a search-and score algorithm that computes scores for nodes and edges and probes orientations of edges to minimize the score.

strengths.value:
The paper proposes a new empirical algorithm for causal structure discovery in ancestral graphs. The practical algorithm is motivated by a theoretical decomposition of likelihood function in terms of multivariate cross-information summed over ac-connected components. The developed algorithm is scalable to graphs with several dozens of vertices and links (thousands of unknown parameters)

The authors provide experimental results on both synthetic datasets and challenging benchmarks from the bnlearn repository, showing that developed algorithm typically has higher precision and similar recall to prior MIIC algorithm.

weaknesses.value:
The proposed algorithm seems to be only empirical and lacks theoretical guarantees and relies on MIIC as a base of the algorithm. To my understanding, the paper does not provide a guarantee that the algorithm always converges in a reasonable number of steps (even if not to a global minimum). Multivariate cross-information over a large set of variables may be very sensitive to noise, which I think is a weakness compared to algorithms that use cross-information only over small number of (e.g. triples) of variables.

Also as the authors point out Theorem 1 is equivalent to the decomposition established in prior work, which makes novelty of the main theorem somewhat questionable.

I also think that it will be beneficial to the reader if the connection between the theoretical results in Theorem 1 and the proposed algorithm are explained a bit more deeply with a more clear connection of how that theorem is being used.

summary.value: The paper defines a score for ancestral graphs through an inclusion-exclusion expansion and implements it into a hybrid search approach.

strengths.value: The likelihood decomposition (Theorem 1) is nice and there seems to be a slight improvement in the empirical testing.

weaknesses.value:
There are close overlaps to published and preprint works by Hu and Evans, so it is hard to assess the novelty here. For example Theorem 1 (in another form) is from reference 14. 

Then in the simulation studies, relevant methods from the references are excluded, even though the greedy search approaches (like references 13 and 32 for example) are not exact, but also heuristic. These (and similar) would need to be included in the benchmarking to judge the importance of the work.

questions.value: Can the authors more clearly delineate what is novel and different here as compared to the other recent works of search-and-score for ancestral graphs?

limitations.value: The limitation on the depth of the inclusion/exclusion is discussed in the limitation section, but maybe this wasn't so clear throughout the paper.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors present a novel likelihood decomposition of ancestral graphs, which is based on a novel concept ac-connected subset. With this decomposition, the authors present an efficient hybrid causal discovery method. But it is worthy to note that in the implementation of the causal discovery method, they use the approximate local scores limited to the closed surrounding vertices of each node and edge, but not the exact likelihood score.

strengths.value:
1. The likelihood decomposition of ancestral graphs is very novel and could be useful in the future.
2. For me, I encourage the studies on the MAG/PAG learning methods. It is a hard and fundamental problem.
3. The paper is clearly written.

questions.value:
1. Could authors elaborate more on where Theorem 1 can be applied?

2. I am curious about how to find ac-connected subset, and what the computational complexity is.

3. One important thing that the readers may wonder is, what is the performance difference between the method based on approximate local scores limited to the closed surrounding vertices and the method with exact scores. Could the authors present more clues?

4. Could the authors present some efficiency comparisons empirically, as the authors say "to implement an efficient and reliable heuristic method applicable to more challenging graphical modes and large datasets". 

I am happy to increase my score if the questions are addressed.

summary.value: Authors propose a greedy structure learning algorithm in the context of ancestral graphs. The score function is based on the normalized likelihood. The score is decomposable using the concept of ac-components. Limited experimental results are presented as experimental evidence.

strengths.value:
- The multivariate cross-entropy decomposition is explained in details, especially the link between its definition and its application in the context of ancestral graphs. Leveraging this framework allows a flexible and effective definition of scoring criteria for the class of graphical models.
- The usage of ac-connecting paths and ac-connected subsets for the likelihood decomposition (theorem 1) is the main result of the paper and allows to map the structure of an ancestral graph to a specific estimand.

weaknesses.value:
- In the case of ancestral graphs, it's crucial to understand the differences between edge patterns. I would suggest to refactor Figure 1 to improve readability, e.g. isolating different edge patterns combinations with horizontal lines.
- The performance of the proposed solution is poor. For instance, Figure 2 most of the metrics overlap with existing solutions.
- The experiments keep the number of samples fixed even is the number of the parameters of the model increase, reducing the information available for the biggest models. Moreover, a sample size of 100 for BARLEY (114,005 parameters) is rather unrealistic.

questions.value:
- Are the limitations related to the cap of two-collider paths only? Are there any issues related to computational complexity? This was partially referenced in the attached form.
- What was the reason of choosing only three models for benchmarks? It is unclear the actual advantage of such approach w.r.t. the existing FCI algorithm.
- Why keeping the sample size range fixed even if the number of possible states increases dramatically? Observing 100 samples for BARLEY means that (ideally) each algorithm observe less than 1% of the state space, which limits the experimental evidence.

limitations.value:
- The experimental evidence is poor: few reference models with rather sparse hyperparameters space exploration.
- The search and score algorithm limits the number of possible exploration paths to the barely minimum.
- It is unclear what is the actual computational burden of the proposed score.

title.value: An efficient search-and-score algorithm for ancestral graphs using multivariate information scores

TLDR.value: We propose an efficient search-and-score algorithm for ancestral graphs based multivariate information scores

abstract.value: We propose a greedy search-and-score algorithm for ancestral graphs, which include directed as well as bidirected edges, originating from unobserved latent variables. The normalized likelihood score of directed mixed graphs is estimated in terms of multivariate information over relevant subsets of variables, ${C}$, that are connected through collider paths confined to the ancestor set of ${C}$. For computational efficiency, the proposed two-step algorithm relies on local information scores limited to the close surrounding variables of each node (step 1)  and edge (step 2). This computational strategy is shown to outperform state-of-the-art causal discovery methods on challenging benchmark datasets.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
